claims.source: We recently showed that immature oligodendrocytes have the capacity to sense neuronal activity and receive glutamatergic inputs in the auditory brainstem (Berret et al., 2017), suggesting that neuron-oligodendrocyte communication occurs through chemical signaling.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that oligodendrocytes receive glutamatergic inputs and express glutamate receptors.

claims.claim: BDNF is highly expressed in MNTB principal neurons.
claims.source: Immunostaining using the neuronal marker MAP2 and the oligodendroglial marker, Olig1, in brainstem sections from wild-type (WT) mice showed that BDNF is highly expressed in MNTB principal neurons (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating BDNF expression in MAP2+ neurons.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocytes located close to the calyx–MNTB neuron synapse express BDNF.
claims.source: It is of note that oligodendrocytes located close to the calyx–MNTB neuron synapse also expressed BDNF.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating BDNF expression in Olig1+ cells near synapses.

claims.claim: BDNF expression was notably decreased in all cell types in the MNTB in Bdnf+/− mice at P21.
claims.source: BDNF expression was notably decreased in all cell types in the MNTB in Bdnf+/−mice at P21 (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A comparing BDNF expression in WT and Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the amplitude of mEPSCs in WT and Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the amplitude or kinetics, including rise and decay times, of mEPSCs in WT and Bdnf+/– mice (amplitude: 39.9 ± 2.51 pA, n = 13 vs 33.4 ± 2.92 pA, n = 12, respectively, p=0.10; rise time: 0.3 ± 0.01 ms, n = 13 vs 0.3 ± 0.02 ms, n = 12, respectively, p=0.37; decay time: 0.6 ± 0.03 ms, n = 13 vs 0.7 ± 0.07 ms, n = 12, respectively, p=0.58, unpaired t-test; Figure 1C–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of mEPSCs showing no statistical difference in amplitude between genotypes.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the rise time of mEPSCs in WT and Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the amplitude or kinetics, including rise and decay times, of mEPSCs in WT and Bdnf+/– mice (amplitude: 39.9 ± 2.51 pA, n = 13 vs 33.4 ± 2.92 pA, n = 12, respectively, p=0.10; rise time: 0.3 ± 0.01 ms, n = 13 vs 0.3 ± 0.02 ms, n = 12, respectively, p=0.37; decay time: 0.6 ± 0.03 ms, n = 13 vs 0.7 ± 0.07 ms, n = 12, respectively, p=0.58, unpaired t-test; Figure 1C–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of mEPSCs showing no statistical difference in rise time between genotypes.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the decay time of mEPSCs in WT and Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the amplitude or kinetics, including rise and decay times, of mEPSCs in WT and Bdnf+/– mice (amplitude: 39.9 ± 2.51 pA, n = 13 vs 33.4 ± 2.92 pA, n = 12, respectively, p=0.10; rise time: 0.3 ± 0.01 ms, n = 13 vs 0.3 ± 0.02 ms, n = 12, respectively, p=0.37; decay time: 0.6 ± 0.03 ms, n = 13 vs 0.7 ± 0.07 ms, n = 12, respectively, p=0.58, unpaired t-test; Figure 1C–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of mEPSCs showing no statistical difference in decay time between genotypes.

claims.claim: The frequency of mEPSCs was not statistically different between WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: In addition, the frequency of mEPSCs was not statistically different (2.7 ± 0.69 Hz, n = 8 vs 2.4 ± 0.41 Hz, n = 11 in WT and Bdnf+/− mice, respectively; p=0.76, unpaired t-test; Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of mEPSCs showing no statistical difference in frequency between genotypes.

claims.claim: The amplitude of evoked EPSCs triggered by afferent fiber stimulation was significantly smaller in Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: However, the amplitude of evoked EPSCs (eEPSCs) triggered by afferent fiber stimulation was significantly smaller in Bdnf+/− mice (3.1 ± 0.31 nA, n = 17 in Bdnf+/− mice vs 5.9 ± 0.35 nA, n = 9 in WT; p<0.0001, unpaired t-test; Figure 1G,H).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of eEPSCs showing statistically significant reduction in amplitude in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The decay time constant of eEPSCs was not significantly different between WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: The line corresponding to eEPSC decay was well fit as a single exponential with a time constant tau (τ)=1.0 ± 0.07 ms (n = 9) in WT and 0.9 ± 0.05 ms (n = 17) in Bdnf+/− mice, which were not significantly different (p=0.31, unpaired t-test; Figure 1G,I).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of eEPSC decay kinetics showing no statistical difference between genotypes.

claims.claim: A reduction in endogenous BDNF results in impaired glutamatergic transmission caused by alterations in presynaptic properties rather than postsynaptic components.
claims.source: These results suggest that a reduction in endogenous BDNF results in impaired glutamatergic transmission, which is caused by alterations in presynaptic properties rather than postsynaptic components.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mEPSC properties (postsynaptic) are unchanged while eEPSC amplitude (presynaptic) is reduced.

claims.claim: The paired pulse ratio was similar in WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: To test the effect of reduced BDNF on presynaptic properties, we examined the paired pulse ratio (PPR), which was similar in both groups (0.8 ± 0.02, n = 9 in WT and 0.8 ± 0.03, n = 17 in Bdnf+/− mice; p=0.93, unpaired t-test; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of paired-pulse responses showing no statistical difference between genotypes.

claims.claim: A reduction in endogenous BDNF does not alter the Ca2+-dependent release probability at presynaptic terminals.
claims.source: This indicates that a reduction in endogenous BDNF does not alter the Ca2+-dependent release probability at presynaptic terminals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that paired-pulse ratio, which reflects release probability, is unchanged in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: There was no notable difference in short-term depression between WT and Bdnf+/− mice during a train of stimuli at 100 Hz.
claims.source: During a train of stimuli at 100 Hz (50 pulses), the amplitude of eEPSCs displayed strong depression, falling to ~20% of the initial amplitude near the end of the train in both WT and Bdnf+/− mice (Figure 2B). There was no notable difference in short-term depression between WT and Bdnf+/− mice (n = 7 vs 12).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings during high-frequency stimulation showing similar depression patterns.

claims.claim: The cumulative eEPSC size estimated by the EQ method was significantly smaller in Bdnf+/− mice compared to WT.
claims.source: We plotted the eEPSC amplitudes during a train versus their cumulative amplitudes at the end of a train (Figure 2C), which were 91.5 ± 9.46 nA (n = 6) in WT and 46.3 ± 6.89 nA (n = 13) in Bdnf+/− mice (p=0.0016, unpaired t-test; Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis using the EQ method showing statistically significant reduction in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: Calyces in Bdnf+/− mice had a much smaller RRP of glutamate vesicles as compared with WT mice as measured by the EQ method.
claims.source: The forward extrapolation linear fits revealed that calyces in Bdnf+/− mice had a much smaller RRP of glutamate vesicles as compared with WT mice (17.6 ± 2.73 nA in Bdnf+/− mice, n = 11 vs 33.4 ± 3.31 nA in WT, n = 5; p=0.004, unpaired t-test; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis using the EQ method showing statistically significant reduction in RRP in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The number of vesicles in the RRP was reduced in Bdnf+/− mice (~527 vesicles) compared to WT (~837 vesicles).
claims.source: The RRP divided by the mEPSC amplitude (Figure 1C) approximately estimates the number of vesicles, which was reduced in in Bdnf+/− mice (~837 vesicles in WT and ~527 vesicles in Bdnf+/− mice).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the RRP size divided by mEPSC amplitude to estimate vesicle number.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in release probability (Pr) between WT and Bdnf+/− mice as determined by the EQ method.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in Pr, determined as the slop of the linear fit (0.25 ± 0.035 in Bdnf+/− mice, n = 10 vs 0.26 ± 0.037 in WT, n = 6; p=0.8582, unpaired t-test; Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis showing no statistical difference in Pr between genotypes.

claims.claim: Calyces in Bdnf+/− mice had a much smaller RRP of glutamate vesicles as compared with WT mice as measured by the SMN method.
claims.source: This analysis also revealed that calyces in Bdnf+/− mice had a much smaller RRP of glutamate vesicles as compared with WT mice (9.8 ± 1.29 nA in Bdnf+/− mice, n = 11 vs 19.4 ± 1.71 nA in WT, n = 5; p=0.0008, unpaired t-test; Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis using the SMN method showing statistically significant reduction in RRP in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The release probability (Pr) calculated by the SMN method was not different in WT and Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.source: Conversely, the release probability (Pr), which is calculated by dividing the amplitude of the first eEPSC by the RRP size, was not different in WT and Bdnf+/– mice (0.35 ± 0.02, n = 5 vs 0.38 ± 0.05, n = 11, respectively, p=0.73, unpaired t-test; Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis showing no statistical difference in Pr between genotypes.

claims.claim: The replenishment rate of vesicles was reduced in Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: Another interesting finding was the reduced replenishment rate of vesicles in Bdnf+/− mice, which was estimated by the slope of the linear fit (0.61 ± 0.10 in Bdnf+/− mice, n = 11 vs 1.39 ± 0.19 in WT, n = 5; p=0.0018, unpaired t-test; Figure 2F), indicating that BDNF signaling plays a role in the replenishment of vesicles at the calyx terminal.
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis showing statistically significant reduction in replenishment rate in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: BDNF signaling plays a role in the replenishment of vesicles at the calyx terminal.
claims.source: Another interesting finding was the reduced replenishment rate of vesicles in Bdnf+/− mice, which was estimated by the slope of the linear fit (0.61 ± 0.10 in Bdnf+/− mice, n = 11 vs 1.39 ± 0.19 in WT, n = 5; p=0.0018, unpaired t-test; Figure 2F), indicating that BDNF signaling plays a role in the replenishment of vesicles at the calyx terminal.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that replenishment rate is reduced when BDNF is reduced.

claims.claim: A reduction in endogenous BDNF decreased the pool of glutamate vesicles available for release at the beginning of a train in Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: Taken together, these results show that a reduction in endogenous BDNF decreased the pool of glutamate vesicles available for release at the beginning of a train in Bdnf+/− mice, suggesting that BDNF is important for determining the RRP at presynaptic terminals.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the cumulative EPSC analysis data showing reduced RRP.

claims.claim: BDNF is important for determining the RRP at presynaptic terminals.
claims.source: Taken together, these results show that a reduction in endogenous BDNF decreased the pool of glutamate vesicles available for release at the beginning of a train in Bdnf+/− mice, suggesting that BDNF is important for determining the RRP at presynaptic terminals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RRP is reduced when BDNF is reduced.

claims.claim: Tetanic stimulation (100 Hz, 3 s) increased the amplitude of eEPSCs in WT mice, indicating PTP induction.
claims.source: Tetanic stimulation (100 Hz, 3 s) increased the amplitude of eEPSCs from 5.6 ± 1.01 pA to 8.0 ± 0.96 pA in WT (n = 5; p=0.02, paired t-test), indicating a PTP induction, whereas there was no significant increase in the eEPSC amplitude after tetanus in Bdnf+/− mice (2.8 ± 0.37 pA to 2.7 ± 0.39 pA, n = 9; p=0.05, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing statistically significant increase in eEPSC amplitude after tetanic stimulation in WT.

claims.claim: There was no significant increase in the eEPSC amplitude after tetanus in Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: Tetanic stimulation (100 Hz, 3 s) increased the amplitude of eEPSCs from 5.6 ± 1.01 pA to 8.0 ± 0.96 pA in WT (n = 5; p=0.02, paired t-test), indicating a PTP induction, whereas there was no significant increase in the eEPSC amplitude after tetanus in Bdnf+/− mice (2.8 ± 0.37 pA to 2.7 ± 0.39 pA, n = 9; p=0.05, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no statistically significant increase in eEPSC amplitude after tetanic stimulation in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: BDNF controls synaptic plasticity as well as neurotransmitter release by regulating the RRP at the calyx terminal.
claims.source: Taken together, BDNF controls synaptic plasticity as well as neurotransmitter release by regulating the RRP at the calyx terminal.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement inferred from the data showing reduced RRP and impaired PTP in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: ΔCm in Bdnf+/− mice was much smaller than that in WT after a 20 ms depolarization.
claims.source: ΔCm in Bdnf+/− mice was much smaller than that in WT (ΔCm after a 20 ms depolarization: 93.4 ± 8.82 fF, n = 11 in Bdnf+/− vs 148 ± 11.32 fF, n = 11 in WT mice; p=0.0013, unpaired t-test; Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by capacitance measurements showing statistically significant reduction in ΔCm in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The membrane capacitances of calyces from WT and Bdnf+/− mice were similar.
claims.source: However, the membrane capacitances of calyces from WT and Bdnf+/− mice were similar (20 ± 1.5 pF, n = 10 vs 21.5 ± 1.35 pF, n = 9, respectively, p=0.43, unpaired t-test; Figure 3C), indicating that the sizes of the calyx terminals are similar, and thus the difference in ΔCm was not due to the terminal size.
claims.evidence: Supported by capacitance measurements showing no statistical difference in resting Cm between genotypes.

claims.claim: The sizes of the calyx terminals are similar in WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: However, the membrane capacitances of calyces from WT and Bdnf+/− mice were similar (20 ± 1.5 pF, n = 10 vs 21.5 ± 1.35 pF, n = 9, respectively, p=0.43, unpaired t-test; Figure 3C), indicating that the sizes of the calyx terminals are similar, and thus the difference in ΔCm was not due to the terminal size.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that membrane capacitance, which reflects terminal size, is similar between genotypes.

claims.claim: The difference in ΔCm was not due to the terminal size.
claims.source: However, the membrane capacitances of calyces from WT and Bdnf+/− mice were similar (20 ± 1.5 pF, n = 10 vs 21.5 ± 1.35 pF, n = 9, respectively, p=0.43, unpaired t-test; Figure 3C), indicating that the sizes of the calyx terminals are similar, and thus the difference in ΔCm was not due to the terminal size.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that terminal size (measured by Cm) is similar while ΔCm is different.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the presynaptic ICa charge (QICa) in response to depolarizing pulses between WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the presynaptic ICa charge (QICa) in response to depolarizing pulses. The smaller ΔCm in calyces from Bdnf+/− mice was not attributed to alterations in presynaptic Ca2+ currents. In WT calyces, a 20 ms depolarization induced a ICa of 6.5 ± 0.53 pC/pF (n = 10), whereas in Bdnf+/− calyces, ICa was 5.9 ± 0.96 pC/pF (n = 9; p=0.50, unpaired t-test; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Ca2+ current measurements showing no statistical difference in QICa between genotypes.

claims.claim: The smaller ΔCm in calyces from Bdnf+/− mice was not attributed to alterations in presynaptic Ca2+ currents.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the presynaptic ICa charge (QICa) in response to depolarizing pulses. The smaller ΔCm in calyces from Bdnf+/− mice was not attributed to alterations in presynaptic Ca2+ currents. In WT calyces, a 20 ms depolarization induced a ICa of 6.5 ± 0.53 pC/pF (n = 10), whereas in Bdnf+/− calyces, ICa was 5.9 ± 0.96 pC/pF (n = 9; p=0.50, unpaired t-test; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ca2+ currents are similar while ΔCm is reduced in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The current–voltage relationship (I–V) curve for voltage-activated Ca2+ channels at the calyx terminal exhibited a similar pattern in WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: In addition, the current–voltage relationship (I–V) curve for these voltage-activated Ca2+ channels at the calyx terminal in WT and Bdnf+/− mice (at P10-12) exhibited a similar pattern with the peak current of −625 ± 48.3 pA vs −614 ± 16.5 pA at −10 mV in WT and Bdnf+/− mice, respectively (n = 15 vs n = 15; Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by Ca2+ current measurements showing similar I-V relationships between genotypes.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in amplitude and half-width of presynaptic action potential between WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, we examined presynaptic action potential evoked by afferent fiber stimulation, and there was no significant difference in amplitude and half-with of presynaptic action potential, which is associated with Ca2+ channel activation and release probability (amplitude, 122.5 ± 7.8 mV in WT, n = 3 vs 124.6 ± 4.4 mV in Bdnf+/−, n = 4, p=0.8082 and half-width, 318 ± 41.2 μs in WT, n = 3 vs 283 ± 45.5 μs in Bdnf+/−, n = 4, p=0.6123, unpaired t-test, data not shown).
claims.evidence: Supported by action potential recordings showing no statistical difference in amplitude or half-width between genotypes.

claims.claim: A reduction in endogenous BDNF decreases exocytosis of vesicular glutamate, but this reduction is not associated with changes in Ca2+ influx via Ca2+ channels at the presynaptic terminals.
claims.source: These data suggest that a reduction in endogenous BDNF decreases exocytosis of vesicular glutamate, but this reduction is not associated with changes in Ca2+ influx via Ca2+ channels at the presynaptic terminals.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement inferred from the data showing reduced ΔCm but unchanged Ca2+ currents in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The accumulated capacitance jump (ΣΔCm) was significantly smaller in Bdnf+/− mice relative to WT.
claims.source: The accumulated capacitance jump (ΣΔCm), which is a measure of the sum of available glutamate vesicles released by stimulation, was significantly smaller in Bdnf+/− mice (260 ± 54.1 fF, n = 9) relative to WT (508 ± 86.2 fF, n = 11; p=0.04, t-test; Figure 3G–I).
claims.evidence: Supported by capacitance measurements during repetitive stimulation showing statistically significant reduction in ΣΔCm in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The endocytosis rate was similar in WT and Bdnf+/− mice.
claims.source: This difference, however, was not associated with the endocytosis rate, which was similar in both groups (19.5 ± 2.75 s, n = 10 in WT vs 17.3 ± 1.91 s, n = 9 in Bdnf+/− mice; p=0.51, unpaired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by capacitance decay measurements showing no statistical difference in endocytosis rate between genotypes.

claims.claim: The decreased ΣΔCm resulted mainly from the reduction in the RRP size in Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.source: Therefore, the decreased ΣΔCm resulted mainly from the reduction in the RRP size in Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ΣΔCm is reduced while endocytosis rate is unchanged in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The endogenous BDNF level is directly involved in glutamatergic transmission based on its ability to determine the RRP size at the presynaptic terminal.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that the endogenous BDNF level is directly involved in glutamatergic transmission based on its ability to determine the RRP size at the presynaptic terminal.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement inferred from the data showing reduced RRP and ΣΔCm in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: TrkB was expressed at the calyx terminal and axon.
claims.source: TrkB was expressed at the calyx terminal and axon, which was immunolabelled with VGluT1 and detected by Alexa 568 dye filling during presynaptic whole-cell recording (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating TrkB expression in calyx terminals.

claims.claim: In WT mice, the pre-application of 20 μM 7,8-DHF to brainstem slices (30 min) had no effect on the amplitude or PPR of eEPSCs.
claims.source: In WT mice, the pre-application of 20 μM 7,8-DHF to brainstem slices (30 min) had no effect on the amplitude (6.6 ± 0.53 nA for control vs 6.3 ± 0.70 nA for 7,8-DHF, n = 5, p=0.70, unpaired t-test) or PPR (0.75 ± 0.03 for control vs 0.74 ± 0.01 for 7,8-DHF, n = 5, p=0.86, unpaired t-test) of eEPSCs (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no statistical difference in eEPSC amplitude or PPR with 7,8-DHF treatment in WT.

claims.claim: In Bdnf+/− mice, TrkB activation using 7,8-DHF significantly increased the amplitude of eEPSCs without changing the PPR.
claims.source: In Bdnf+/− mice, TrkB activation using 7,8-DHF significantly increased the amplitude of eEPSCs (from 2.8 ± 0.54 nA, n = 8 to 4.5 ± 0.40 nA, n = 17, p=0.02, unpaired t-test) without changing the PPR (0.7 ± 0.05 for control, n = 8 vs 0.8 ± 0.03 for 7,8-DHF, n = 17, p=0.58, unpaired t-test; Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing statistically significant increase in eEPSC amplitude with 7,8-DHF treatment in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: Acute application of 7,8-DHF increased the amplitude of eEPSCs during the 10 min after its application in Bdnf+/− mice in a time-dependent manner.
claims.source: Acute application of 7,8-DHF also increased the amplitude of eEPSCs during the 10 min after its application in Bdnf+/− mice in a time-dependent manner (2.8 ± 0.97 nA for control, n = 5 vs 3.9 ± 1.14 nA for 7,8-DHF at 10 min vs, n = 5, p=0.023, paired t-test; Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing statistically significant increase in eEPSC amplitude over time with acute 7,8-DHF application in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The pre-application of 7,8-DHF significantly increased the cumulative eEPSC size and partially restored the RRP in Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.source: In addition, the pre-application of 7,8-DHF significantly increased the cumulative eEPSC size (from 45.9 ± 7.9 nA, n = 11 to 75.2 ± 9.7 nA, n = 6; p=0.03, unpaired t-test) and partially restored the RRP in Bdnf+/– mice (from 17.6 ± 2.73 nA, n = 11 to 27.8 ± 3.64 nA, n = 7; p=0.03; unpaired t-test, Figure 4F,G).
claims.evidence: Supported by cumulative EPSC analysis showing statistically significant increase in cumulative eEPSC size and RRP with 7,8-DHF treatment in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: The down-regulation of BDNF–TrkB signaling at the presynaptic terminal impairs the RRP size and glutamatergic transmission in the MNTB.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the down-regulation of BDNF–TrkB signaling at the presynaptic terminal impairs the RRP size and glutamatergic transmission in the MNTB.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TrkB agonist rescues deficits in Bdnf+/- mice.

claims.claim: A number of oligodendrocytes are apposed to the calyx synapse in the MNTB during postnatal development.
claims.source: A number of oligodendrocytes are apposed to the calyx synapse in the MNTB during postnatal development (Figures 1A and 5A; Berret et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining images and citation to previous study showing oligodendrocyte proximity to synapses.

claims.claim: Cnpcre is specific to oligodendrocytes and is not expressed in neurons or astrocytes in the MNTB of the auditory brainstem.
claims.source: GFP+ cells were positive for Olig2 and were present next to the calyx synapse, but did not express MAP2, NeuN, and GFAP expression in the MNTB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This confirms that Cnpcre is specific to oligodendrocytes and is not expressed in neurons or astrocytes in the MNTB of the auditory brainstem.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing Cnpcre-driven reporter expression in Olig2+ cells but not in MAP2+, NeuN+, or GFAP+ cells.

claims.claim: Most CNP+ cells in the MNTB are pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes beyond the precursor stage.
claims.source: In addition, CNP+ cells were positive for CC1, but negative for PDGFRa, indicating that most CNP+ cells in the MNTB are pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes beyond the precursor stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing CNP+ cells are CC1+ (mature oligodendrocytes) but not PDGFRα+ (oligodendrocyte precursors).

claims.claim: The sorted O1+ or GFP+ fraction expressed a substantial level of Bdnf in control mice, whereas the O1+ or GFP+ fraction from Bdnf cKO mice showed significantly reduced level of Bdnf.
claims.source: Utilizing quantitative PCR, we confirmed that the sorted O1+ or GFP+ fraction expressed a substantial level of Bdnf in control mice (Cnpcre:Bdnffl/+), whereas the O1+ or GFP+ fraction from Bdnf cKO mice showed significantly reduced level of Bdnf (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by qPCR data from FACS-sorted oligodendrocytes showing reduced Bdnf mRNA in cKO mice.

claims.claim: The deletion of BDNF in oligodendrocytes significantly decreased exocytosis of glutamate vesicles at the calyx terminal in brainstem slices from Bdnf cKO mice.
claims.source: The deletion of BDNF in oligodendrocytes significantly decreased exocytosis of glutamate vesicles at the calyx terminal in brainstem slices from Bdnf cKO mice. In P9–12 Bdnf cKO mice, ΔCm in response to a 2-, 3-, 5-, 10-, 20-, or 40 ms depolarization was much smaller than in control mice (for 20 ms, 123 ± 20 fF for Bdnf cKO, n = 19 vs 266 ± 35.4 fF for the control, n = 20; p=0.0016, unpaired t-test, Figure 5D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by capacitance measurements showing statistically significant reduction in ΔCm in Bdnf cKO mice.

claims.claim: In both control and Bdnf cKO genotypes, the Cm and the Ca2+ influx during depolarizing pulses were similar.
claims.source: In both genotypes, the Cm (15 ± 1.9 pF, n = 14 for control vs 15 ± 3.5 pF, n = 17 for Bdnf cKO; Figure 5F) and the Ca2+ influx during depolarizing pulses were similar (the QICa for 20 ms was 5.1 ± 0.45 pC/pF, n = 13 for the control vs 5.5 ± 0.39 pC/pF, n = 11 for the Bdnf cKO; p=0.45, unpaired t-test; Figure 5G), indicating that the loss of oligodendroglial BDNF impairs vesicular exocytosis without a change in Ca2+ channel activation, similar to what was observed in Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by capacitance and Ca2+ current measurements showing no statistical difference between control and cKO mice.

claims.claim: The loss of oligodendroglial BDNF impairs vesicular exocytosis without a change in Ca2+ channel activation.
claims.source: In both genotypes, the Cm (15 ± 1.9 pF, n = 14 for control vs 15 ± 3.5 pF, n = 17 for Bdnf cKO; Figure 5F) and the Ca2+ influx during depolarizing pulses were similar (the QICa for 20 ms was 5.1 ± 0.45 pC/pF, n = 13 for the control vs 5.5 ± 0.39 pC/pF, n = 11 for the Bdnf cKO; p=0.45, unpaired t-test; Figure 5G), indicating that the loss of oligodendroglial BDNF impairs vesicular exocytosis without a change in Ca2+ channel activation, similar to what was observed in Bdnf+/– mice.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ΔCm is reduced while Ca2+ currents are unchanged in Bdnf cKO mice.

claims.claim: The current–voltage relationship (I–V) curve for voltage-activated Ca2+ channels at the calyx terminal exhibited a similar pattern in control and Bdnf cKO mice.
claims.source: In addition, the current–voltage relationship (I–V) curve for these voltage-activated Ca2+ channels at the calyx terminal in control and Bdnf cKO mice (at P10-12) exhibited a similar pattern with the peak current of −633 ± 35.4 pA vs −540 ± 107.1 pA at −10 mV in control and Bdnf cKO mice, respectively (n = 4 vs 5; Figure 5H).

results.result: BDNF is expressed in both MNTB principal neurons and oligodendrocytes near the calyx-MNTB synapse in wild-type mice, with expression notably decreased in all cell types in Bdnf+/− mice at P21.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1A) showing BDNF expression in MAP2+ neurons and Olig1+ oligodendrocytes in WT mice, with reduced expression in Bdnf+/− mice. The immunofluorescence evidence directly demonstrates the cellular localization and genotype-dependent expression of BDNF.

results.result: Reduction of endogenous BDNF in Bdnf+/− mice significantly decreases evoked EPSC amplitude without affecting miniature EPSC properties (amplitude, kinetics, frequency) or evoked EPSC decay kinetics, indicating impaired glutamatergic transmission due to presynaptic rather than postsynaptic alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are well-supported by electrophysiological recordings showing unchanged mEPSC properties (p>0.05 for all comparisons) but significantly reduced eEPSC amplitude (p<0.0001) in Bdnf+/− mice. The inference that deficits are presynaptic (C32) is logically sound given that postsynaptic measures (mEPSCs) are unaffected while evoked responses are impaired.

results.result: Reduction in endogenous BDNF does not alter paired-pulse ratio or short-term depression, indicating that Ca2+-dependent release probability at presynaptic terminals is unchanged in Bdnf+/− mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by electrophysiological data showing similar PPR (p=0.93) and short-term depression patterns between WT and Bdnf+/− mice. The inference that release probability is unchanged (C34) is appropriate given that PPR is a standard measure of release probability.

results.result: Reduction in endogenous BDNF significantly decreases the readily releasable pool (RRP) of glutamate vesicles and vesicle replenishment rate in Bdnf+/− mice without altering release probability, as measured by both EQ and SMN methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C45 are strongly supported by cumulative EPSC analysis using two independent methods (EQ and SMN). Both methods show statistically significant reductions in RRP (p=0.004 and p=0.0008 respectively) and replenishment rate (p=0.0018), while release probability remains unchanged (p>0.05). The convergence of two analytical approaches strengthens the conclusion that BDNF regulates RRP size.

results.result: Tetanic stimulation induces post-tetanic potentiation (PTP) in WT mice but not in Bdnf+/− mice, indicating that BDNF controls synaptic plasticity and neurotransmitter release by regulating the RRP at the calyx terminal.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by electrophysiological data showing significant PTP induction in WT (p=0.02) but not in Bdnf+/− mice (p=0.05). The inference that BDNF controls plasticity through RRP regulation (C48) is reasonable given the established link between RRP size and PTP, though the mechanism could be further validated.

results.result: Reduction in endogenous BDNF significantly decreases membrane capacitance changes (ΔCm) reflecting reduced vesicular glutamate exocytosis in Bdnf+/− mice, without altering terminal size, Ca2+ currents, or action potential properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 are well-supported by capacitance measurements showing significantly reduced ΔCm (p=0.0013) while resting Cm, Ca2+ currents (QICa), I-V relationships, and action potential properties remain unchanged (all p>0.05). This dissociation between exocytosis and Ca2+ influx is critical evidence that BDNF acts downstream of Ca2+ entry.

results.result: The accumulated capacitance jump (ΣΔCm) during repetitive stimulation is significantly reduced in Bdnf+/− mice without changes in endocytosis rate, indicating that decreased ΣΔCm results from reduced RRP size and that endogenous BDNF is directly involved in determining RRP size at presynaptic terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by capacitance measurements showing significantly reduced ΣΔCm (p=0.04) with unchanged endocytosis rate (p=0.51). The inference that reduced ΣΔCm results from reduced RRP (C60) is logical given the unchanged endocytosis, and the conclusion about BDNF's role (C61) is consistent with all preceding data.

results.result: TrkB is expressed at calyx terminals, and TrkB activation using 7,8-DHF significantly increases eEPSC amplitude and partially restores RRP in Bdnf+/− mice without affecting WT mice, indicating that down-regulation of BDNF-TrkB signaling impairs RRP size and glutamatergic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by immunostaining showing TrkB expression (C62) and electrophysiological data showing that 7,8-DHF rescues deficits in Bdnf+/− mice (p=0.02 for eEPSC amplitude, p=0.03 for RRP) without affecting WT mice (p>0.05). This pharmacological rescue provides strong evidence for TrkB-mediated signaling.

results.result: Oligodendrocytes are apposed to calyx synapses during postnatal development, and Cnpcre is specific to oligodendrocytes (not neurons or astrocytes) in the MNTB, with most CNP+ cells being pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes that express substantial Bdnf mRNA, which is significantly reduced in Bdnf cKO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by immunostaining showing oligodendrocyte proximity to synapses (C68), specificity of Cnpcre expression in Olig2+ but not MAP2+/NeuN+/GFAP+ cells (C69), CC1+/PDGFRα− phenotype indicating pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes (C70), and qPCR data from FACS-sorted cells showing reduced Bdnf in cKO oligodendrocytes (C71). These data validate the conditional knockout model.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte-specific deletion of BDNF significantly decreases exocytosis of glutamate vesicles (ΔCm and ΣΔCm) at calyx terminals without altering terminal size, Ca2+ influx, or endocytosis rate, indicating that oligodendrocytes are critically involved in determining presynaptic RRP and vesicular glutamate release through BDNF signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are strongly supported by capacitance measurements in Bdnf cKO mice showing significantly reduced ΔCm (p=0.0016) and ΣΔCm (p=0.006) with unchanged Cm, QICa, I-V curves, and endocytosis rate (all p>0.05). This recapitulation of the Bdnf+/− phenotype with oligodendrocyte-specific deletion provides compelling evidence for oligodendrocyte-derived BDNF's role.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte-specific BDNF deletion significantly impairs eEPSC amplitude and RRP at both immature (P10-12) and mature (P16-20) calyx synapses without affecting PPR or release probability, indicating that oligodendroglial BDNF is important for regulating glutamatergic transmission before and after hearing onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are supported by electrophysiological recordings at two developmental stages showing significantly reduced eEPSC amplitude (p=0.032 at P10-12, p<0.0001 at P16-20) and RRP (p=0.0238 and p=0.0004 respectively) with unchanged PPR and Pr (all p>0.05). The developmental persistence of deficits strengthens the conclusion about oligodendroglial BDNF's importance.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte-specific BDNF deletion significantly decreases the number of docked vesicles within 10 nm of the active zone at both immature and mature calyx synapses without affecting terminal volume or clustered vesicles within 200 nm, indicating that oligodendroglial BDNF signaling is important for mobilizing glutamate vesicles at presynaptic terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are supported by electron microscopy showing significantly reduced docked vesicles in Bdnf cKO mice (p=0.0285 at P10-12, p<0.0001 at P20) with unchanged terminal volume (p=0.3308) and clustered vesicles (p=0.26). This ultrastructural evidence provides direct anatomical support for the functional RRP deficits observed electrophysiologically.

results.result: Application of the TrkB agonist 7,8-DHF recovers the reduced number of docked vesicles at active zones in Bdnf cKO mice, indicating that activation of BDNF-TrkB signaling rescues the vesicle docking/mobilization defect and RRP reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by electron microscopy showing that 7,8-DHF treatment restores docked vesicle numbers in Bdnf cKO mice to control levels. This pharmacological rescue at the ultrastructural level provides strong evidence that TrkB activation is sufficient to restore vesicle mobilization.

results.result: Exogenous BDNF or TrkB agonist (7,8-DHF) application significantly increases ΔCm and ΣΔCm in Bdnf cKO mice without affecting Ca2+ currents or control mice, indicating that oligodendrocyte-derived BDNF activates presynaptic TrkB signaling to modulate RRP and enhance glutamatergic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C100 are well-supported by capacitance measurements showing that both BDNF and 7,8-DHF significantly increase ΔCm (p=0.04 for both) and ΣΔCm (p=0.001 and p=0.008 respectively) in Bdnf cKO mice without affecting QICa (p>0.05) or control mice. This pharmacological rescue provides strong evidence for the BDNF-TrkB signaling mechanism.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte-specific BDNF deletion does not affect ABR thresholds, wave I amplitude, or conduction latencies, but significantly reduces amplitudes of central ABR waves II-IV (particularly wave III), indicating impaired neuronal activity and synaptic synchrony in central auditory nuclei and demonstrating that oligodendroglial BDNF critically influences auditory transmission during postnatal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C108 are supported by ABR recordings showing unchanged thresholds and peripheral measures (wave I, latencies; all p>0.05) but significantly reduced central wave amplitudes (wave III p=0.002). This selective impairment of central auditory responses provides important in vivo functional validation of the synaptic deficits observed in vitro, demonstrating physiological relevance.

results.result: Oligodendrocytes modulate neurotransmitter release at presynaptic terminals through BDNF secretion, which functions via presynaptic TrkB to reduce the readily releasable pool of glutamate vesicles without altering Ca2+ channel activation or release probability, and this effect is recapitulated by oligodendrocyte-specific BDNF deletion and rescued by BDNF or TrkB agonist application.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 and C115 represent the main conclusions of the study and are supported by the convergence of multiple experimental approaches: immunostaining, electrophysiology, capacitance measurements, electron microscopy, conditional knockout mice, pharmacological rescue, and in vivo ABR recordings. The consistency of results across these diverse methodologies provides strong support for the central thesis.

results.result: Background knowledge establishing that oligodendrocytes near synapses detect neuronal activity, express neurotransmitter receptors, and secrete BDNF; that BDNF regulates neuronal survival, synaptic transmission, and plasticity; and that glial cells (including oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglia) modulate synaptic properties through BDNF secretion, though the specific role of oligodendrocytes in synapse development and the source of BDNF at synapses remain largely unexplored.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C22 and C109-C114 represent established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims provide the necessary context and rationale for the current study. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field's understanding.
